title: How do you perform a stream-to-stream join in Flink SQL (`SELECT ... FROM orders o JOIN shipments s ON o.order_id = s.order_id WHERE ...`), and why must you specify a time constraint (`AND o.order_time BETWEEN s.ship_time - INTERVAL '4' HOUR AND s.ship_time`) to bound state?
shortTitle: How do you perform a stream-to-stream join in Flink SQL and why bound state with a time constraint

s1_definition.profdef: A stream-to-stream join in Flink SQL matches rows from two unbounded streaming tables on a join key, producing enriched rows when a match is found. Because both sides are unbounded, a plain equi-join would require Flink to keep every row from both streams in state forever so that a future row on either side could still find its partner, which makes state grow without limit. An interval join adds a time constraint in the WHERE or ON clause, such as `o.order_time BETWEEN s.ship_time - INTERVAL '4' HOUR AND s.ship_time`, which tells Flink that a match can only occur within a bounded time window, so once the watermark passes that window the engine can safely evict old rows and keep state finite.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has two live feeds. One feed is payment orders that Rajesh submits, and the other feed is the settlement confirmations that come back from the clearing house. To pair each order with its confirmation, we join the two feeds on the order id. If we never said how long to wait, the bank would have to remember every order forever just in case a confirmation showed up years later, which fills up the vault of memory. So we say a confirmation can only arrive within four hours of the order. After four hours the bank can forget that order, because no valid confirmation will ever match it, and memory stays under control.
s1_definition.oneliner: A stream-stream join without a time bound keeps state forever, so you add an interval constraint to let watermarks evict old rows and keep state finite.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A stream-to-stream join in Flink SQL matches rows from two unbounded streaming tables on a join key, producing enriched rows when a match is found. Because both sides are unbounded, a plain equi-join would require Flink to keep every row from both streams in state forever so that a future row on either side could still find its partner, which makes state grow without limit. An interval join adds a time constraint in the WHERE or ON clause, such as `o.order_time BETWEEN s.ship_time - INTERVAL '4' HOUR AND s.ship_time`, which tells Flink that a match can only occur within a bounded time window, so once the watermark passes that window the engine can safely evict old rows and keep state finite.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has two live feeds. One feed is payment orders that Rajesh submits, and the other feed is the settlement confirmations that come back from the clearing house. To pair each order with its confirmation, we join the two feeds on the order id. If we never said how long to wait, the bank would have to remember every order forever just in case a confirmation showed up years later, which fills up the vault of memory. So we say a confirmation can only arrive within four hours of the order. After four hours the bank can forget that order, because no valid confirmation will ever match it, and memory stays under control.

**One line to remember:** A stream-stream join without a time bound keeps state forever, so you add an interval constraint to let watermarks evict old rows and keep state finite.

sections.s2_technical:
In Flink SQL both tables in a join are dynamic tables backed by continuous sources such as Kafka topics. When you write a regular join, for example `FROM orders o JOIN shipments s ON o.order_id = s.order_id`, Flink produces a regular stream join. To guarantee that a row arriving on either side can be matched against any past or future row on the other side, Flink stores every row it has seen from both inputs in keyed state. This is correct but the state grows forever because nothing tells Flink that an old order can never match a new shipment, so for unbounded streams this is usually unacceptable in production.

The fix is an interval join, which you express by adding a time predicate relating the two sides' time attributes. For example `AND o.order_time BETWEEN s.ship_time - INTERVAL '4' HOUR AND s.ship_time` says the order time must fall within the four hours before the ship time. Both `order_time` and `ship_time` must be event-time attributes with watermarks defined. Now Flink knows that for a given shipment, only orders within a four-hour band can match, so once the watermark advances past the upper bound of possible matches for a row, that row can be dropped from state. The result is bounded state proportional to the join window size times the event rate, not to the entire history.

You write the time attributes and watermarks in the CREATE TABLE DDL, for example `order_time TIMESTAMP(3), WATERMARK FOR order_time AS order_time - INTERVAL '5' SECOND`. The interval predicate can be symmetric, such as within thirty minutes either side, or asymmetric, such as the order must precede the shipment by at most four hours, which matches real causality. The senior nuances are these. First, choose the interval to cover the real-world maximum lag plus a safety margin, because a match that falls outside the window is silently not produced. Second, watermarks drive eviction, so if a source stalls and its watermark does not advance, state can still grow because Flink cannot prove old rows are safe to drop. Third, an interval join emits an append-only stream, which is cheaper downstream than a retract stream. Fourth, if you genuinely need a regular unbounded join, you must configure a state time-to-live with `table.exec.state.ttl` as a blunt safety net, accepting that very late matches will be missed. Knowing when to use an interval join versus a temporal join versus a lookup join is what separates a real Flink engineer from someone who only writes batch SQL.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs two live streams, a stream of payment orders and a stream of settlement confirmations from the clearing house, and the operations desk needs each order paired with its confirmation so they can report settled versus pending payments in real time. If the pairing logic remembered every order forever, the memory of the matching service would grow until it crashed. This is exactly a stream-stream join, and it needs a time bound so old unmatched orders are forgotten.

Problem 2 — A confirmation normally arrives within four hours of the order; anything later is an operational exception handled by a different process, not a normal match. This is exactly the interval predicate that bounds the join state, because it encodes the real business rule that a match can only happen within four hours.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that mimics an interval join without a Flink cluster, so the logic is visible. We define an `Order` with an order id, account id, amount, and order time, and a `Shipment` which here represents a settlement confirmation with an order id and a ship time. An `IntervalJoinEngine` buffers orders, matches each incoming confirmation to an order whose time falls inside the four-hour window, emits the joined result, and evicts orders once a simulated watermark passes the point where they can no longer match, so you can watch state shrink. An `IntervalJoinDemo` main class feeds a sequence of orders and confirmations, advances the watermark, and prints matches plus the current state size so the bounded-state behavior is obvious.

```
flink-interval-join-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/flink/ij/
│   │   │   ├── IntervalJoinDemo.java          (main runnable demo)
│   │   │   ├── Order.java                     (left stream event)
│   │   │   ├── Shipment.java                  (right stream event = settlement)
│   │   │   └── IntervalJoinEngine.java        (buffers, joins, evicts)
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── query.sql
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/flink/ij/
│           └── IntervalJoinEngineTest.java
```

The SQL this demo models:

```sql
-- query.sql
-- orders and shipments are Kafka-backed dynamic tables with event-time + watermark
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.account_id,
    o.amount,
    o.order_time,
    s.ship_time
FROM orders AS o
JOIN shipments AS s
  ON o.order_id = s.order_id
 AND o.order_time BETWEEN s.ship_time - INTERVAL '4' HOUR AND s.ship_time;
```

Configuration:

```yaml
# application.yml — Flink job config that the SQL above runs under
flink:
  parallelism: 4
  state-backend: rocksdb
  checkpoint:
    interval-ms: 60000
    mode: EXACTLY_ONCE
  table:
    exec-state-ttl: 5h   # safety net slightly larger than the 4h interval
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two streams. Orders: ORD-1 for SAV2001 of fifty thousand at one hour, ORD-2 for CUR3001 of twelve thousand at two hours. Confirmations: ORD-1 at three hours, ORD-2 at eight hours. The interval is four hours.

Step 1. ORD-1 arrives and is buffered in keyed state. State now holds one order. The data lives in the engine's order map keyed by order id.

Step 2. ORD-2 arrives and is buffered. State holds two orders. Nothing has been emitted yet because no confirmation has arrived.

Step 3. The confirmation for ORD-1 arrives at three hours. The engine computes the window, which is the confirmation time minus four hours up to the confirmation time, so from minus one hour to three hours. ORD-1's order time of one hour falls inside, so a joined row is emitted carrying the order fields plus the ship time. The order stays in state for now because a late duplicate confirmation is still theoretically possible until the watermark moves.

Step 4. The confirmation for ORD-2 arrives at eight hours. The window is four to eight hours. ORD-2's order time of two hours is before four hours, so it is outside the interval and no match is produced. This is the business rule working: a confirmation more than four hours late is not a normal settlement match.

Step 5. The watermark advances to six hours. The engine checks each buffered order: ORD-1's order time plus four hours is five hours, which is less than six, so ORD-1 can never match a future confirmation and is evicted. State shrinks to one order. ORD-2 remains because its order time plus four hours is six hours, not strictly less than six.

Step 6. The watermark advances to nine hours. Now ORD-2's order time plus four hours is six hours, which is less than nine, so ORD-2 is evicted. State is empty. The key lesson is visible: state did not grow forever; the time constraint let the watermark clean it up.

Final output:

```
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    buffered order ORD-1 amount=50000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    buffered order ORD-2 amount=12000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    JOINED order=ORD-1 account=SAV2001 amount=50000 shipTime=10800000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    Result: JOINED order=ORD-1 account=SAV2001 amount=50000 shipTime=10800000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 WARNING order ORD-2 outside 4h interval; no match
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    Result: null
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    Evicted at wm=6h: 1
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    State now holds: [ORD-2]
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    Evicted at wm=9h: 1

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A stream-to-stream join in Flink SQL matches rows from two unbounded streaming tables on a join key, and the critical thing to understand is state management. If I write a plain equi-join between two streams, Flink must keep every row from both sides in keyed state indefinitely, because a row arriving far in the future could still match an old row on the other side. For unbounded streams that means state grows without limit and the job eventually fails. The solution is an interval join, where I add a time constraint relating the two sides' event-time attributes, for example the order time must fall within the four hours before the ship time. That predicate tells Flink the maximum possible lag between a match, so once the watermark advances past the point where a row could still find a partner, Flink evicts it and state stays bounded.

The mechanics rest on event time and watermarks. Both time columns are declared as event-time attributes with watermarks in the CREATE TABLE DDL, and the watermark is what drives eviction, because it is Flink's proof that no earlier event will still arrive. I choose the interval to cover the real maximum business lag plus a safety margin, because any genuine match that falls outside the window is silently dropped. The senior points I always mention are that a stalled source whose watermark does not advance will prevent eviction and let state grow even with an interval, that an interval join conveniently produces an append-only stream which is cheaper downstream than a retract stream, and that if I truly need an unbounded regular join I must set a state time-to-live as a blunt safety net and accept missing very late matches.

At the National Bank of India we had exactly this situation with a payment orders stream and a settlement confirmations stream from the clearing house. The operations desk needed every order paired with its confirmation in real time to report settled versus pending payments. I wrote an interval join keyed on the order id with the predicate that the order time must be within four hours of the confirmation time, which matched the real operational rule that a valid confirmation always comes back within four hours. That single predicate turned an unbounded, ever-growing join into one with bounded state that the watermark cleaned up continuously, so the job ran stably for months. I could show the behaviour concretely: a confirmation within four hours produced a joined row, one that arrived six hours late produced no match and flowed to an exception process, and once the watermark passed each order's window the order left state and memory dropped. Being able to explain why unbounded join state is the trap, how the interval predicate plus watermarks fix it, and how I picked the window from the real business lag is exactly what demonstrates production Flink experience rather than textbook knowledge.

---

keyPoints: Structured Streaming: micro-batch or continuous processing
Watermark: handle late data — discard after threshold
Checkpoint: fault tolerance — recover state on failure
